subject: Critical Thinking
title: Induction: From Specific to General
description: A micro-lesson that makes Induction: From Specific to General usable.

hook.text: Every swan you've ever seen is white. So all swans must be white. Welcome to induction — and its dangers.

buildup.text: Inductive reasoning observes specific cases and forms general conclusions. Science runs on it.

discovery.text: Unlike deduction, induction never gives certainty — only probability. More evidence = stronger conclusion.

twist.text: Europeans were certain all swans were white. Then they reached Australia and found black ones.

climax.text: Every scientific law is inductive — it holds until someone finds an exception.

punchline.text: Induction makes us confident. Never certain.

quiz.question: What level of certainty does inductive reasoning provide?

details.summary: Inductive reasoning draws general conclusions from specific observations, providing probable rather than certain conclusions. It is the foundation of scientific inquiry and everyday generalization.
details.whyItMatters: Nearly all empirical knowledge relies on induction, making its strengths and limitations essential to understand for scientific literacy.
takeaways: Induction moves from observations to general conclusions
Sample size from diverse conditions strengthens inductive arguments

faq.question: Why can inductive conclusions never be certain?
faq.answer: No matter how many confirming observations you collect, a future observation could always contradict the pattern. One black swan disproves 'all swans are white.'

faq.question: What makes one inductive argument stronger than another?
faq.answer: Larger, more diverse samples with consistent results produce stronger inductive arguments. A conclusion from thousands of varied cases is more reliable than one from a handful.
